newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Conservatives could hold March election.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Conservatives could hold March election.

text.p: Senior figures in Britain's ruling Conservative Party were on Friday said to be preparing for an early election after the sudden death of a member of parliament pushed Prime Minister John Major's government into a minority.

The Daily Telegraph said Major still favoured holding out until May 1 but he was being pressed by senior Conservatives to consider bringing the election further forward. Major must call an election by May 22 at the latest.
The Telegraph, which has good connections in the Conservative Party, said there were "unmistakeable signs that the election pace was hotting up".
Iain Mills, a rank-and-file Conservative member of parliament, was found dead on Thursday, reducing Major's strength in the lower House of Commons to 322 against 323 members of opposition parties.
Major now leads Britain's first minority government since just before the Conservatives came to power in 1979.
Labour has vowed to force Major out if it can persuade the collection of minority parties in parliament to back it on a key issue. But there is no sign of such an issue on the horizon.
The Telegraph said that by bringing forward the election, Major would be able to choose his own date rather than be forced out by a no-confidence vote in the Commons.
The report coincided with publication of an opinion poll showing the opposition Labour Party 18 points ahead of the Conservatives, but with its lead reduced by six points over the past month.
A Gallup survey for the Telegraph put Labour on 50.5 percent with the Conservatives on 32.5 percent, while the minority Liberal Democrats were trailing at 10.5 percent.

But month-on-month comparisons were affected by the fact that Gallup has changed its method of testing opinion since its last poll for the Telegraph. It has moved to random telephone sampling after having used face-to-face interviews for years.
The Telegraph said the old method of street interviews tended to exaggerate Labour support at the expense of the Conservatives because it reached too many working class voters.
Gallup estimates that Labour's lead has shrunk by six points over the past month with the Conservatives up four points from 28.5 percent and Labour down two points from 52.5 percent.
Support for the Liberal Democrats has fallen by one point over the past month, according to survey in which Gallup interviewed 987 people by telephone between January 11 and 15.
"The poll indicates that the Tories (Conservatives) have got the better of the unofficial election campaign that has been raging since the start of the year," the Telegraph said.
Labour spokesman Brian Wilson said comparison with the December figures could not be treated as valid.

"Effectively, this is a new poll conducted using relatively untried methodology. It should therefore be compared not with the December Gallup poll, but the polls carried out over the last month by other polling organisations in other newspapers."
The most recent poll by ICM put Labour 17 points ahead, while Opinion Research Business gave Labour a 19-point lead.
Labour needs a 4.3 percent swing from the Conservatives at the election to obtain an overall majority. The swing at present, according to Friday's poll, is 12.8 percent to Labour.
